questions.stem: What is the difference between mechanical and chemical digestion?

options.text: Mechanical digestion only occurs in the stomach
Mechanical digestion physically breaks food into smaller pieces; chemical digestion uses enzymes to break chemical bonds
Mechanical digestion uses enzymes; chemical digestion uses teeth

questions.explanation: Mechanical digestion physically breaks food into smaller pieces (e.g., by teeth or churning), increasing surface area. Chemical digestion uses enzymes to break the chemical bonds in food molecules.
Starch digestion begins in the mouth, where salivary amylase starts to break down starch into maltose. This process stops in the acidic stomach and continues in the small intestine.

questions.stem: Why does the stomach produce hydrochloric acid?

options.text: To provide the optimum pH for pepsin and to kill bacteria in food

questions.explanation: Hydrochloric acid in the stomach creates an acidic environment (pH ~2) that is the optimum pH for the protease enzyme pepsin and helps kill harmful bacteria in food.

questions.stem: What role does bile play in digestion?

options.text: It emulsifies fats into smaller droplets, increasing surface area for lipase

questions.explanation: Bile is not an enzyme. It emulsifies (breaks up) large fat globules into smaller droplets, increasing the surface area available for lipase enzymes to break down the fat.

questions.stem: Which enzyme breaks down proteins into amino acids?
questions.explanation: Protease enzymes (such as pepsin in the stomach and trypsin from the pancreas) break down proteins into smaller peptides and eventually into individual amino acids.

questions.stem: What are the final products of lipid digestion?
questions.explanation: Lipase enzymes break down lipids (fats) into fatty acids and glycerol, which are small enough to be absorbed through the wall of the small intestine.

questions.stem: Why is it important that food is broken into small, soluble molecules?

options.text: So the stomach can hold more food
So molecules are small enough to pass through the intestinal wall into the blood

questions.explanation: Food must be broken into small, soluble molecules so they can pass through the wall of the small intestine by diffusion or active transport and enter the bloodstream for distribution to cells.
